title: "AI Alignment"
description: "The study and practice of making AI systems behave in accordance with intended goals and constraints."
term: "AI Alignment"
letter: "A"
category: "AI Safety"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

AI alignment is the work of making an AI system's behaviour match what
people intend, including its goals, constraints, and values, especially in
situations that were not anticipated during development.

## Technical explanation

Alignment spans research and engineering approaches for specifying desired
behaviour, training models toward it, evaluating failures, and controlling
deployed systems. Methods include human feedback, preference learning,
interpretability, robustness work, policy enforcement, and oversight. No
single method fully solves alignment.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A system can perform well on its training objective yet behave poorly in
real use if that objective is incomplete or its operating conditions
change. Alignment concerns help teams reason about misuse, unintended
outputs, over-reliance, and whether a deployment's safeguards match its
capabilities.

## How it works

Teams translate intended behaviour into training signals, system constraints,
and evaluation cases. They test normal and adversarial scenarios, analyze
failures, and refine the model or surrounding controls. Alignment is
iterative because specifications and environments are imperfect.

## Practical example

A coding assistant may be trained to follow user instructions while being
evaluated for whether it respects repository boundaries, avoids exposing
secrets, and asks for confirmation before destructive changes.

## Common misconceptions

- Alignment is broader than preventing harmful text output.
- A high benchmark score does not establish that a system is aligned.
- Alignment is not achieved solely by adding a system prompt or a refusal
  rule.
